Human Trafficking: For Sale

By: Annalise Lubbe | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We take to the streets of Brooklyn where young girls walk the beat. Forced to sell their bodies, modern day slaves to be sold over and over again.

Summary:
It is Tuesday night close to 9h00 in Brooklyn. Slowly the streets take on a life of it's own. From dark alleyways and side streets, figures emerge in Koeberg road, the main artery that connects the veins of the northern suburb of Cape Town.
Known as the hot spot that lures the seedier side of life, here you will find the action: illegals, pimps, prostitutes, drug lords, addicts and girls from all ages waiting to be picked up.
Tonight is no different. We scout the streets with the Vice Squad, Cape Town's special Anti Trafficking Unit, on one of their regular raids. They plan to get more inside information from the girls walking the beat, their whereabouts and why they are here.
We slow down the mini van and stop next to one of the girls standing alone, perhaps 17 or even younger, wearing heels and a short skirt. Officer Jacobs heading the 6-member Vice Squad team asks her name: "Lisa", she says in a soft voice. She is reluctant to answer any other questions beside her age being 23.
"You know prostitution is illegal," says Jacobs in a warning tone to Lisa who is clearly lying about her name and age. Her slow speech and movements is an indication of being high on some form of drug. After a while Lisa admits to selling sex. The female officer in the unit speaks to her in a kind voice to try and coax more information from her that could lead us to her trafficker or pimp.
We found out Lisa was recruited by a woman she became acquainted with back at her hometown in the Eastern Cape. The recruiter promised Lisa 'work' in Cape Town and offered her a lift and a place to stay.
From here the story is almost identical to hundred's of women across South Africa who fall victim. They are mostly from small towns, poor family and not much hope for a better life or further education.



Further information:
As predicted Lisa took the bait. Once she arrived in Cape Town she was introduced to a young attractive man (her trafficker) who traded her cell phone for a new one (with key numbers stored including his own and the recruiter), clothes and drugs to break her spirit and leave her dependent. After a number of days she was ordered by her trafficker to start working to earn her keep and pay back her debt.
Lisa was trapped. She was now in debt bondage to her trafficker. She is under his control, his commodity and he will sell her over and over again. Lisa will take on a pseudo name, never see her ID book again and hand over every cent of her earnings to her trafficker. She will not identify her informer or her address to the Vice Squad in fear of the consequences for her and her family back home.

Sadly less than 1% of cases like Lisa are ever reported. With a low reporting rate comes a low conviction rate. Topped with the slow progress in the TIP Act (The Prevention and Combating of Trafficking in Person's Bill passed in 2013), and no centralised database on national level, South Africa still has a long way to go to meet international standards.
Human Trafficking is the third most lucrative crime in the world after narcotics and guns. It is a multi-billion rand industry preying on the innocent. It is organised, it is a business and it is the selling of human beings - a case of supply versus demand. It is happening right here in our major cities and towns. Every day victims fall pray to modern day slavery. Few victims survive.
Lisa had a chance that night but she did not take it in fear of the consequences. If Lisa went with the Vice Squad, she would have been taken to a Safe House to recover from her traumatic experience. It will be many months before she will be ready to testify in court.
In court she will come face to face with the trafficker again, a secondary traumatic experience that will shut out the cognitive part of her brain. Her memory will lapse. Her story will change and no conviction will be made.

Our Story:
Our story will follow a typical night on an operation in Brooklyn with the crew and presenter under the protection of the Vice Squad. We will speak to the young prostitutes, perhaps see ask what brought them to the city. The story will be told through strong graphic visuals of the seedy side of life in paradox to the young and vulnerable lured and trapped in a web of deceit.
From Brooklyn we will expose other 'hot spots' in Cape Town where prostitution is rife. We get a bird's eye view of what is happening under our eyes every day, every minute. When money is exchanged for sexual favours to the John's of the world through pimps who sell the girls as commodities: young, old,local, foreign, a 'taste' to satisfy every menu.
Our lead case study will be a survivor now living in Khayelitsha with her mother and small son. Grizelda Grootboom (her real name) landed in hospital after she lost her baby and could not work on the streets any longer. She was beaten senseless. Her ordeal in Benoni where she was locked up and sold for sex lasted several months. Today she has picked up the pieces and is able to speak about it.
In April Grizelda's entrapment of eighteen years as a prostitute and being trafficked will be published in her book titled EXIT: "A life that lacked connection with anything meaningful, other than my drugs, my men, prostitution", she writes. She was one of the lucky few who got out to tell the story.
Many victims stay trapped. They have to choose between a life back home where poverty and abuse is often all they know and a seemingly caring trafficker who 'looks after their needs': from their drug addiction to a roof over their head, clothes and food. They call it the Stockholm syndrome where the trafficker assumes the role of a care-giver. One of the girls who were rescued and placed in a safe house told the house mother: "he buys me clothes, he looks after me," holding up one of the many items still with price tags from her suitcase.

I visualise the story being told through the victims and the survivor to give a true reflection of human trafficking on our doorstep.

Key questions we ask in this story:
Why and how do young women end up on the street in bondage?
What legal recourse do the victims have?
Is there a lifeline and help readily available for victims who want to escape?
Are the fines hefty enough for perpetrators of Human Trafficking?

Interviews:
Victims: Questioning by the Vice Squad to the prostitutes
Survivor: Formal interview with Grizelda on camera telling her story of the places she frequented, the streets she walked and type of customers she had. Visuals of the some of the places in Cape Town will be captured. We will show her modest home in Khayelitsha and talk about her story on the road to recovery as told in her book. (the book will not form the focal point)

Organisations and caregivers:
Interview with A21, an international NGO working with the victims to assist the Vice Squad on rescue and placement at a Safe House.
A possible interview with a mother of a Safe House or a Social Worker who can talk us through the recovery process

Government:
We will speak to a legal expert on the TIP Act and ask if progress has been made in bringing perpetrators of human trafficking to book and what is the success rate.

Vice Squad:
The key person who will be questioning the prostitutes will be miked and all answers of the girls will be on boom.
They will talk about their role in identifying, assisting and reporting of cases of Human Trafficking.

Viewing Notes:
FOR SALE/TRAFFICKING VIEWING 1 26/04/2016 12:06:27 PM Present:Duncan/Tumi GM AC WG

Will you make the changes and set up a second viewing please – and well done, overall we thought it was a great story, nice elements and we were impressed considering this is your first CB story:

1. Start with the vice squad operation and shorten it and then get into the narrative of Grizelda
2. Explain that while there are women willingly working in brothels this is also where they go to find women who are working there against their will – this is how they find victims who are exploited and don’t have the means to come forward. Give a clear sense that these women are being exploited rather than they are there willingly – like the massage queen woman who is there willingly to make a living as a hooker
3. Explain that their ID is taken, they are given another phone etc spell out the facts
4. Grizelda – there isn’t any evidence that she was trafficked, who trafficked her, you need to set her up more. We need a great deal more about her to understand what actually happened to her. We need to hear more of her narrative from her. Can you tell us which hospital she ended up in, show the hospital, talk more about how her journey of recovery has taken a long time.
5. It worries us that she has laid no charges – Annalise says she is in a desperate state and so didn’t go to police, many victims never report it – we need to corroborate what she has said and show the physical places where these things occurred.
6. Trafficking context widely locally and internationally: You need to add in more about trafficking otherwise this story is about prostitution. Add in international and local stats that show that this is an international problem and happening right here in SA.
7. There are some places in the script where ‘was/were’ are incorrect in sentences – please check grammar
8. Can you add in comment from
9. What is A21? You show them very briefly so explain them or leave them out.
10. You will change the voice of the prostitute on the street who talks about the brothers’ in the area and so she doesn’t want to talk
11. The ending is very abrupt you need something more concluding from Grizelda.
12. Embrace dignity would be useful as they can talk about the patterns of human trafficking and why we should believe Grizelda.
LEGAL FEEDBACK – DUNCAN / THUMI
1. The last two girls arrested at the end - the blurring wasn’t comprehensive enough and also the women on the couch in the brothel upfront and some other scenes in the brothel ensure extra blurring – and were there any clients in there? Cant show their faces either.
2. The crimes were not described clearly – where she spoke about the TIP act
3. We agree Grizelda could be telling the truth but we have to show that we took reasonable steps – its best to try to take some steps ourselves rather than rely on Jacana publishers’ checking. Solve this by going to the places where she says it happened and show that these are the places where she says it happened. Go through the physical evidence – the house, the hospital, anyone else she dealt with who can corroborate what she is saying. You may not be able to prove every fact but you need to find facts that we can check and if those don’t add up that’s a problem but if most of them do then we can say we did what we could.

Press Release:


Vice Squad Crack Down: Human Trafficking
Carte Blanche joins the Vice Squad on a raid to crack down on organised crime that is flourishing as a result of the trafficking of young women. We also meet Grizelda Grootboom, a brave victim of trafficking who survived to share her gruelling story.


Script:


Carte Blanche: FOR SALE
10 MAY 2016
Presenter: John Webb
Duration: 10 minutes
Text
V/O Tonight we are on patrol in Cape Town with the Vice Squad and the HAWKS on a special operation to expose sex trafficking.
Nathan Ladegourdie: John, we receive information regarding a massage parlour that is operating as a brothel and we are going to send in an undercover agent.
Link: Well we are about a block away from the premises. The hawks and the Vice Squad are on standby. They have sent an agent into the building and if his request for sex is agreed to that is when they will swoop.
John: Well Nathan we have got confirmation there.
Nathan: Yes John we got confirmation the undercover operation was a success.
V/O We count about 12 young women in the brothel and several clients in the waiting. It was in this room no. 2 that the undercover agent was offered sex.
Up audio: “Ek is opgesluit vir prostitusie”. (“I am locked up for prostitution”)
V/O The prostitute who offered sex and the front desk manager who received payment from the undercover agent was taken into custody.
John: It is becoming quite clear that in order to police human trafficking you have to police a whole set of other crimes as well.
Nathan: We address human trafficking by concentrating on street prostitution and your brothels and between those ladies you will find those that are forced into the sex trade.
V/O Prostitutes who act voluntary have a choice. With victims of trafficking, there is no choice. Women are exploited for sex to make money for their trafficker with little chance of escape.
V/O We are in Bellville, a suburb north of Cape Town where girls, some barely 18, are waiting to be picked up with only a pocket of condemns for protection.
V/O Globally an estimated 20.9 million adults and children are sold into sexual slavery and forced labour. Women and girls make up 80% of victims.
Accurate statistics are virtually impossible as traffickers operate below the radar. Less than 1% of victims are rescued.

V/O Grizelda Grootboom was barely 18 years old when she was trafficked. Her story began in Woodstock where she grew up with her father.
Grizelda: He was that shield he was that man in my life that carried me on his shoulders all the time and walking through the streets of Woodstock.
V/O At 9 she was forced to go and live with her mother in Khayeltisha after her dad had lost his job.
Grizelda: Being with my mom was very confusing because there was no words that we said to each other. It was like I am disturbing her household I am disturbing her family.
V/O Then the most disturbing thing happened to the young Grizelda. She was gang raped by boys from her neighbourhood.
John: I guess you could not talk to your mom?
Grizelda: No. There was nobody I could talk to there was nobody that wanted to know what I went through so.
John: After that you left Khayelitsha eventually, where did you go?
Grizelda: I started joining the rest of the street kids and stayed under the bridge until I got to a point that I met a lot of girls and they said usually they go this orphan house.
V/O The orphanage, was little more than a roof over her head. The streets were the bonding ground.
Grizelda: I grew a friendship with one of the girls that I met on the street and enjoyed our drugs and our supplies. I felt like she knew me very very well.
V/O The first sign of trafficking is to build trust with the unsuspecting victim and to know her circumstances. The friend, a student from Johannesburg who lived in Yeoville, spoke about jobs and promised Grizelda a room of her own.
Grizelda: That sounded so friendly, so welcoming. I was like, yes thank you so much. I have somebody I can count on.

V/O The second element of trafficking is deception and the abuse of power over the vulnerable state of the victim. Grizelda arrived in Yeoville and was shown her room. Then her friend left.
Grizelda: The last time I saw her she said she was going to get me something to eat and I just slept and trusting her once more.
V/O When Grizelda woke up, 2 men entered the room. They taped her eyes shut and tied her hands.
Grizelda: My eyes were blurry and not awake, and the first thing was a budge. And then just being punched and undressed and stomach punches and the whole body went numb.

John: That must have been horrific not being able to see what was happening around you?
Grizelda; Yes it was. A lot of stuff was just painful.
V/O The third element of trafficking is exploitation of the victim often through severe sexual violence and assault.
John: So in effect you were being kept as a prisoner, you had a tape over your eyes, pumped full of drugs. How many men do you think came each day?

Grizelda: Well in the mornings there would be about 5 because you could smell them being fresh. In the evening you can count about 11 or 12.
John: How would you deal with something so horrendous?
Grizelda: I did. I always just use to think of, most of the time my dad carrying me on his shoulders. Whenever I feel that a client is choking me in his pleasuring moment and would just hold my breath so I can faint.
V/O At the end of two weeks Grizelda was thrown out on the streets. Traumatised and hooked on drugs she knew only one way to survive. Her fate might have been different had she known about a place of safety. The Carte Blanche crew were given special permission to enter this safe-house for victims as its location is a closely guarded secret.
Miryam Cherpillod: So every time we have a young woman coming through our doors its always very emotional. Some are affected by the use of drugs through their years of exploitation others have huge health issues.

V/O S-Cape is one of about 30 safe houses in South Africa. Since opening their door in 2011 they have helped over 60 victims.
Miryam: As they start getting trust again slowly they start opening up there is little windows of hope for their life that maybe that wasn’t the end of the road for them.
V/O The journey to recovery is long and complex. The Department of Social Services plays a key role in victim empowerment.
Buti Kulwane: We have developed what we call the Restoration and Healing Programme, in addition to looking at the person’s pshycho-social need it also looks at their physical needs, provides education on their rights and also on their behaviour. You are looking at an individual who was through a trafficking traumatised.
V/O In South Africa there were 205 victims of human trafficking reported between April 2014 and December 2015.
In Africa, 8,215 and globally 33,024 for 2015.
Link: Previously Human Trafficking cases were of prosecuted with different pieces of legislation. The new Act came into affect in August last year and it is hoped will strengthen the hand of prosecutors and the police to ensure that perpetrators are brought to book.
Dawn Coleman-Malinga: For us the act creates a specific offense of TIP but also for other related offenses in the act like debt bondage and possession and destruction documentation, utilising a person or benefitting financially from the trafficked victim.
V/O. The maximum sentence for human trafficking is R100 million or life imprisonment or both.
Dawn: I don’t think we will ever comprehend what most of the victims have gone through. They have been raped 20 to 30 times a day.
V/O Back on the streets of Bellville it was past midnight. This young woman told us that her ID was taken away and her simcard replaced with a new number the trafficker is using to sell her online.
Officer: Who’s got your id?
Prostitute: Him
Officer: What did he do with your simcard?
Prostitute: He take it. He said that number…he gave me the new one.
Link: after a very long night the Vice Squad had come across a lady who appears on the surface at least to be prostituting against her will. But despite their best efforts she has turned down their help.
Officer: If I offer you help, will you go with me?
Prostitute: I can’t. I am scare to make a statement because some of his brothers, they are around here.
V/O For Grizelda, her life reached a turning point when she was forced into the abortion at 3 months of a baby she planned to call Summer.
John: Do you ever think of summer?
Grizelda; I think about Summer all the time. And her just being a baby girl in my presence what was I going to teach her and what kind of mother was I going to be. And sometimes I regret because just seeing summer in the sink I regret that I have this life.
V/O It took years before Grizelda was ready to come forward and tell her story. Embrace Dignity has been part of that journey.
Surya: Grizelda blocked the story for a very long time and it took courage of her to really start sharing. And it will for every survivor to share because it is about trust and for that person to take responsibility because it is not only me blaming my what happened to me but it is I am taking my life back, I am taking ownership and responsibility.
V/O To this day Grizelda is still not naming the trafficker. Despite having written her book she still fears the consequences.
Surya: She has decided to rather write about the story, to tell the story on various platforms and she is currently using the book at schools to share her story in prisons and the general public.
V/O Life has gone a full circle. Grizelda has returned to her mother’s home in Khyaelitsha.
Grizelda: And our relationship strengthens. And every time I come back and she says I am so proud of you. And then just opening the room and having a cooked meal from my mom and having that fragrance in the house. It’s the best. She is amazing yeh.

We also meet Grizelda Grootboom, a brave victim of trafficking who survived to share her gruelling story. Script: Carte Blanche: FOR SALE 10 MAY 2016 Presenter: John Webb Duration: 10 minutes Text V/O Tonight we are on patrol in Cape Town with the Vice Squad and the HAWKS on a special operation to expose sex trafficking. Nathan Ladegourdie: John, we receive information regarding a massage parlour that is operating as a brothel and we are going to send in an undercover agent. Link: Well we are about a block away from the premises. The hawks and the Vice Squad are on standby. They have sent an agent into the building and if his request for sex is agreed to that is when they will swoop. John: Well Nathan we have got confirmation there. Nathan: Yes John we got confirmation the undercover operation was a success. V/O We count about 12 young women in the brothel and several clients in the waiting. It was in this room no. 2 that the undercover agent was offered sex. Up audio: “Ek is opgesluit vir prostitusie”. (“I am locked up for prostitution”) V/O The prostitute who offered sex and the front desk manager who received payment from the undercover agent was taken into custody. John: It is becoming quite clear that in order to police human trafficking you have to police a whole set of other crimes as well. Nathan: We address human trafficking by concentrating on street prostitution and your brothels and between those ladies you will find those that are forced into the sex trade. V/O Prostitutes who act voluntary have a choice. With victims of trafficking, there is no choice. Women are exploited for sex to make money for their trafficker with little chance of escape. V/O We are in Bellville, a suburb north of Cape Town where girls, some barely 18, are waiting to be picked up with only a pocket of condemns for protection. V/O Globally an estimated 20.9 million adults and children are sold into sexual slavery and forced labour. Women and girls make up 80% of victims. Accurate statistics are virtually impossible as traffickers operate below the radar. Less than 1% of victims are rescued. V/O Grizelda Grootboom was barely 18 years old when she was trafficked. Her story began in Woodstock where she grew up with her father. Grizelda: He was that shield he was that man in my life that carried me on his shoulders all the time and walking through the streets of Woodstock. V/O At 9 she was forced to go and live with her mother in Khayeltisha after her dad had lost his job. Grizelda: Being with my mom was very confusing because there was no words that we said to each other. It was like I am disturbing her household I am disturbing her family. V/O Then the most disturbing thing happened to the young Grizelda. She was gang raped by boys from her neighbourhood. John: I guess you could not talk to your mom? Grizelda: No. There was nobody I could talk to there was nobody that wanted to know what I went through so. John: After that you left Khayelitsha eventually, where did you go? Grizelda: I started joining the rest of the street kids and stayed under the bridge until I got to a point that I met a lot of girls and they said usually they go this orphan house. V/O The orphanage, was little more than a roof over her head. The streets were the bonding ground. Grizelda: I grew a friendship with one of the girls that I met on the street and enjoyed our drugs and our supplies. I felt like she knew me very very well. V/O The first sign of trafficking is to build trust with the unsuspecting victim and to know her circumstances. The friend, a student from Johannesburg who lived in Yeoville, spoke about jobs and promised Grizelda a room of her own. Grizelda: That sounded so friendly, so welcoming. I was like, yes thank you so much. I have somebody I can count on. V/O The second element of trafficking is deception and the abuse of power over the vulnerable state of the victim. Grizelda arrived in Yeoville and was shown her room. Then her friend left. Grizelda: The last time I saw her she said she was going to get me something to eat and I just slept and trusting her once more. V/O When Grizelda woke up, 2 men entered the room. They taped her eyes shut and tied her hands. Grizelda: My eyes were blurry and not awake, and the first thing was a budge. And then just being punched and undressed and stomach punches and the whole body went numb. John: That must have been horrific not being able to see what was happening around you? Grizelda; Yes it was. A lot of stuff was just painful. V/O The third element of trafficking is exploitation of the victim often through severe sexual violence and assault. John: So in effect you were being kept as a prisoner, you had a tape over your eyes, pumped full of drugs. How many men do you think came each day? Grizelda: Well in the mornings there would be about 5 because you could smell them being fresh. In the evening you can count about 11 or 12. John: How would you deal with something so horrendous? Grizelda: I did. I always just use to think of, most of the time my dad carrying me on his shoulders. Whenever I feel that a client is choking me in his pleasuring moment and would just hold my breath so I can faint. V/O At the end of two weeks Grizelda was thrown out on the streets. Traumatised and hooked on drugs she knew only one way to survive. Her fate might have been different had she known about a place of safety. The Carte Blanche crew were given special permission to enter this safe-house for victims as its location is a closely guarded secret. Miryam Cherpillod: So every time we have a young woman coming through our doors its always very emotional. Some are affected by the use of drugs through their years of exploitation others have huge health issues. V/O S-Cape is one of about 30 safe houses in South Africa. Since opening their door in 2011 they have helped over 60 victims. Miryam: As they start getting trust again slowly they start opening up there is little windows of hope for their life that maybe that wasn’t the end of the road for them. V/O The journey to recovery is long and complex. The Department of Social Services plays a key role in victim empowerment. Buti Kulwane: We have developed what we call the Restoration and Healing Programme, in addition to looking at the person’s pshycho-social need it also looks at their physical needs, provides education on their rights and also on their behaviour. You are looking at an individual who was through a trafficking traumatised. V/O In South Africa there were 205 victims of human trafficking reported between April 2014 and December 2015. In Africa, 8,215 and globally 33,024 for 2015. Link: Previously Human Trafficking cases were of prosecuted with different pieces of legislation. The new Act came into affect in August last year and it is hoped will strengthen the hand of prosecutors and the police to ensure that perpetrators are brought to book. Dawn Coleman-Malinga: For us the act creates a specific offense of TIP but also for other related offenses in the act like debt bondage and possession and destruction documentation, utilising a person or benefitting financially from the trafficked victim. V/O. The maximum sentence for human trafficking is R100 million or life imprisonment or both. Dawn: I don’t think we will ever comprehend what most of the victims have gone through. They have been raped 20 to 30 times a day. V/O Back on the streets of Bellville it was past midnight. This young woman told us that her ID was taken away and her simcard replaced with a new number the trafficker is using to sell her online. Officer: Who’s got your id? Prostitute: Him Officer: What did he do with your simcard? Prostitute: He take it. He said that number…he gave me the new one. Link: after a very long night the Vice Squad had come across a lady who appears on the surface at least to be prostituting against her will. But despite their best efforts she has turned down their help. Officer: If I offer you help, will you go with me? Prostitute: I can’t. I am scare to make a statement because some of his brothers, they are around here. V/O For Grizelda, her life reached a turning point when she was forced into the abortion at 3 months of a baby she planned to call Summer. John: Do you ever think of summer? Grizelda; I think about Summer all the time. And her just being a baby girl in my presence what was I going to teach her and what kind of mother was I going to be. And sometimes I regret because just seeing summer in the sink I regret that I have this life. V/O It took years before Grizelda was ready to come forward and tell her story. Embrace Dignity has been part of that journey. Surya: Grizelda blocked the story for a very long time and it took courage of her to really start sharing. And it will for every survivor to share because it is about trust and for that person to take responsibility because it is not only me blaming my what happened to me but it is I am taking my life back, I am taking ownership and responsibility. V/O To this day Grizelda is still not naming the trafficker. Despite having written her book she still fears the consequences. Surya: She has decided to rather write about the story, to tell the story on various platforms and she is currently using the book at schools to share her story in prisons and the general public. V/O Life has gone a full circle. Grizelda has returned to her mother’s home in Khyaelitsha. Grizelda: And our relationship strengthens. And every time I come back and she says I am so proud of you. And then just opening the room and having a cooked meal from my mom and having that fragrance in the house. It’s the best. She is amazing yeh. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We take to the streets of Brooklyn where young girls walk the beat. Forced to sell their bodies, modern day slaves to be sold over and over again.
metadata.Summary: It is Tuesday night close to 9h00 in Brooklyn. Slowly the streets take on a life of it's own. From dark alleyways and side streets, figures emerge in Koeberg road, the main artery that connects the veins of the northern suburb of Cape Town. Known as the hot spot that lures the seedier side of life, here you will find the action: illegals, pimps, prostitutes, drug lords, addicts and girls from all ages waiting to be picked up. Tonight is no different. We scout the streets with the Vice Squad, Cape Town's special Anti Trafficking Unit, on one of their regular raids. They plan to get more inside information from the girls walking the beat, their whereabouts and why they are here. We slow down the mini van and stop next to one of the girls standing alone, perhaps 17 or even younger, wearing heels and a short skirt. Officer Jacobs heading the 6-member Vice Squad team asks her name: "Lisa", she says in a soft voice. She is reluctant to answer any other questions beside her age being 23. "You know prostitution is illegal," says Jacobs in a warning tone to Lisa who is clearly lying about her name and age. Her slow speech and movements is an indication of being high on some form of drug. After a while Lisa admits to selling sex. The female officer in the unit speaks to her in a kind voice to try and coax more information from her that could lead us to her trafficker or pimp. We found out Lisa was recruited by a woman she became acquainted with back at her hometown in the Eastern Cape. The recruiter promised Lisa 'work' in Cape Town and offered her a lift and a place to stay. From here the story is almost identical to hundred's of women across South Africa who fall victim. They are mostly from small towns, poor family and not much hope for a better life or further education.
metadata.Further information: As predicted Lisa took the bait. Once she arrived in Cape Town she was introduced to a young attractive man (her trafficker) who traded her cell phone for a new one (with key numbers stored including his own and the recruiter), clothes and drugs to break her spirit and leave her dependent. After a number of days she was ordered by her trafficker to start working to earn her keep and pay back her debt. Lisa was trapped. She was now in debt bondage to her trafficker. She is under his control, his commodity and he will sell her over and over again. Lisa will take on a pseudo name, never see her ID book again and hand over every cent of her earnings to her trafficker. She will not identify her informer or her address to the Vice Squad in fear of the consequences for her and her family back home. Sadly less than 1% of cases like Lisa are ever reported. With a low reporting rate comes a low conviction rate. Topped with the slow progress in the TIP Act (The Prevention and Combating of Trafficking in Person's Bill passed in 2013), and no centralised database on national level, South Africa still has a long way to go to meet international standards. Human Trafficking is the third most lucrative crime in the world after narcotics and guns. It is a multi-billion rand industry preying on the innocent. It is organised, it is a business and it is the selling of human beings - a case of supply versus demand. It is happening right here in our major cities and towns. Every day victims fall pray to modern day slavery. Few victims survive. Lisa had a chance that night but she did not take it in fear of the consequences. If Lisa went with the Vice Squad, she would have been taken to a Safe House to recover from her traumatic experience. It will be many months before she will be ready to testify in court. In court she will come face to face with the trafficker again, a secondary traumatic experience that will shut out the cognitive part of her brain. Her memory will lapse. Her story will change and no conviction will be made. Our Story: Our story will follow a typical night on an operation in Brooklyn with the crew and presenter under the protection of the Vice Squad. We will speak to the young prostitutes, perhaps see ask what brought them to the city. The story will be told through strong graphic visuals of the seedy side of life in paradox to the young and vulnerable lured and trapped in a web of deceit. From Brooklyn we will expose other 'hot spots' in Cape Town where prostitution is rife. We get a bird's eye view of what is happening under our eyes every day, every minute. When money is exchanged for sexual favours to the John's of the world through pimps who sell the girls as commodities: young, old,local, foreign, a 'taste' to satisfy every menu. Our lead case study will be a survivor now living in Khayelitsha with her mother and small son. Grizelda Grootboom (her real name) landed in hospital after she lost her baby and could not work on the streets any longer. She was beaten senseless. Her ordeal in Benoni where she was locked up and sold for sex lasted several months. Today she has picked up the pieces and is able to speak about it. In April Grizelda's entrapment of eighteen years as a prostitute and being trafficked will be published in her book titled EXIT: "A life that lacked connection with anything meaningful, other than my drugs, my men, prostitution", she writes. She was one of the lucky few who got out to tell the story. Many victims stay trapped. They have to choose between a life back home where poverty and abuse is often all they know and a seemingly caring trafficker who 'looks after their needs': from their drug addiction to a roof over their head, clothes and food. They call it the Stockholm syndrome where the trafficker assumes the role of a care-giver. One of the girls who were rescued and placed in a safe house told the house mother: "he buys me clothes, he looks after me," holding up one of the many items still with price tags from her suitcase. I visualise the story being told through the victims and the survivor to give a true reflection of human trafficking on our doorstep. Key questions we ask in this story: Why and how do young women end up on the street in bondage? What legal recourse do the victims have? Is there a lifeline and help readily available for victims who want to escape? Are the fines hefty enough for perpetrators of Human Trafficking? Interviews: Victims: Questioning by the Vice Squad to the prostitutes Survivor: Formal interview with Grizelda on camera telling her story of the places she frequented, the streets she walked and type of customers she had. Visuals of the some of the places in Cape Town will be captured. We will show her modest home in Khayelitsha and talk about her story on the road to recovery as told in her book. (the book will not form the focal point) Organisations and caregivers: Interview with A21, an international NGO working with the victims to assist the Vice Squad on rescue and placement at a Safe House. A possible interview with a mother of a Safe House or a Social Worker who can talk us through the recovery process Government: We will speak to a legal expert on the TIP Act and ask if progress has been made in bringing perpetrators of human trafficking to book and what is the success rate. Vice Squad: The key person who will be questioning the prostitutes will be miked and all answers of the girls will be on boom. They will talk about their role in identifying, assisting and reporting of cases of Human Trafficking. ______________________________________________________
